direct_use_loci.text: [F7] Continuous real functions on Euclidean space are Borel measurable; sums, products, scalar multiples and absolute values of Borel measurable real functions are Borel measurable; a function that agrees on an open set with a continuous function and is constant on the complementary closed set is Borel measurable; every Borel subset of Euclidean space is Lebesgue measurable. direct_use_loci.text: For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

direct_use_loci.text: The two factors of the $k$th summand are $\mathcal F_k$-measurable because $\mathcal F_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal F_k$. Measurable arithmetic [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] makes the product measurable; it is integrable by hypothesis. Every finite sum is therefore $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and integrable by the locally reconstructed linearity (the unaffected remainder of [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]] gives the same calculation). At zero the sum is empty and equals zero.

direct_use_loci.text: For a centered triangular array as in [[def-row-wise-independent-centered-triangular-array]], suppose every entry has finite second moment. Write $$v_{n,k}=\mathbb E_nX_{n,k}^2=\operatorname{Var}_n(X_{n,k}),\qquad s_n^2=\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}v_{n,k}.$$ Variance is defined in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Every term is finite and nonnegative, so the finite sum and its nonnegative square root s_n exist. Whenever $s_n>0$, define $$L_n(\varepsilon)=s_n^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}\mathbb E_n\!\left[X_{n,k}^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_{n,k}|>\varepsilon s_n\}}\right]\quad(\varepsilon>0).$$ The **Lindeberg condition** is $L_n(\varepsilon)\to0$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, with $s_n>0$ for all n under consideration. The event is measurable because absolute value is continuous and the entries are measurable; products are measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Its nonnegative integrand is bounded by $X_{n,k}^2$, so its expectation exists and is finite by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. In particular $0\le L_n(\varepsilon)\le1$.

direct_use_loci.text: The threshold event is measurable because $X$ is measurable and $[-A,A]$ is Borel; its indicator and the product are measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Since $|X^{(A)}|\le A$, for every $0<p<\infty$ its absolute $p$th moment is at most $A^p\mathbb P(\Omega)=A^p$. This is not clipping to the endpoints.

Cauchy–Schwarz with the constant one gives $E|Y_k|\le(EY_k^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Repeated use of $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ shows that every finite sum $S_n$ has finite second moment, and hence finite first moment. Group independence and [F2] give $E[Y_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=0$, while the known $S_n$ conditions to itself. Thus $E[S_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=S_n$, proving the martingale property [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4]

direct_use_loci.text: [F9] Absolute values of measurable real functions are measurable. A statement holding almost surely has a measurable null exceptional set. The probability measure satisfies $P(\Omega)=1$. For nonnegative measurable $g$, the set function $B\mapsto\int_B g\,dP$ is a measure; the nonnegative integral is monotone under pointwise order, indicators integrate to their measures, and integrals over null sets vanish. A real measurable function is integrable exactly when its absolute-value integral is finite ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[def-probability-measure]], [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

direct_use_loci.text: [F3] $(t,x)\mapsto\sum_{j\in F}\varepsilon_j(t)\Delta_jf(x)$ is measurable on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^n$: it is a finite sum of products of Borel functions of $t$ with continuous functions of $x$ ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]); hence $|{\cdot}|^p$ of it is nonnegative and product-measurable, and Tonelli's theorem applies, in particular $\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\cdot|^pdx\,dt=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\int_0^1|\cdot|^pdt\,dx$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

direct_use_loci.text: [F9] For $c\in\mathbb R$, the translation $t\mapsto t-c$ is Borel measurable because its strict upper threshold set at $a$ is $(a+c,\infty)$. For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, the map $t\mapsto e^{\lambda t}$ is Borel measurable: its upper threshold set is $\mathbb R$ for $a\le0$; for $a>0$ it is $\mathbb R$ if $\lambda=0$ and $a<1$, empty if $\lambda=0$ and $a\ge1$, $(\log(a)/\lambda,\infty)$ if $\lambda>0$, and $(-\infty,\log(a)/\lambda)$ if $\lambda<0$. These formulas use $\exp(0)=1$, positivity, strict increase, and the inverse relation of $\exp$ and $\log$. Borel maps preserve measurability under composition, and finite arithmetic and lattice operations preserve measurability ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

direct_use_loci.text: 1.1 By [[thm-monotone-functions-are-differentiable-almost-everywhere-via-rising-sun]], $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$. Extend $F$ to $[a,b+1]$ by setting $\widetilde F(x)=F(x)$ for $x \le b$ and $\widetilde F(x)=F(b)$ for $x \ge b$. For each $n \ge 1$ define $h_n(x) := n\bigl(\widetilde F(x+1/n)-\widetilde F(x)\bigr)$ for $x \in [a,b]$. Because monotone functions are Borel measurable ([[thm-monotone-real-functions-are-borel-measurable]]) and arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]), each $h_n$ is measurable and nonnegative. At every point where $F'$ exists, $h_n(x) \to F'(x)$. [given, construct]
